title: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
summary: How unikernels link one application with only the OS code it needs into one VM image, how they run requests and move packets, what they gain, and how they compare with Linux-based alternatives.
outcomes: Explain why a single-application VM does not need a user/kernel split and what isolation the hypervisor provides instead
Compute the speedup from turning syscalls into function calls for a given request profile, and its limits
Describe how micro-libraries, static linking and dead code elimination produce a small specialized image
Explain how a single-vCPU unikernel serves many requests with an event loop or cooperative threads, and why fork is missing
Trace a packet through a virtio split virtqueue and count the notifications a batch of packets costs
Explain where unikernel boot time goes, and measure it with kraft or mirage on a real VMM
Decide when a unikernel fits a service, weighing security, compatibility, debugging and porting costs
Place unikernels among OSv, Lupine, UKL, Firecracker microVMs and gVisor, and pick one for a workload

lessons.title: One app, two isolation layers: why a whole OS is redundant

blocks.md:
A typical cloud server is one application, say a DNS server or nginx, inside a virtual machine (VM). The VM boots a full general-purpose OS: a kernel, a C library, a shell, cron, package tooling, and the application. The hypervisor (the software that splits one physical machine into many VMs, like Xen or KVM, the kernel-based virtual machine built into Linux) already isolates this VM from every other tenant.

Inside the VM, the guest kernel then isolates the application from... nothing else. There is only one application. Yet every read, write and send still crosses the user/kernel boundary you met in the system calls course, paying a mode switch each time.

A **unikernel** removes that inner layer. Madhavapeddy and colleagues coined the term in their 2013 paper at ASPLOS (the Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems conference): a *specialised, sealed, single-purpose library OS VM that runs directly on the hypervisor*. Sealed means the image cannot change its own code once it is running; lesson 5 shows how. The paper built **Mirage** (now MirageOS), a unikernel written entirely in OCaml, a memory-safe functional language, so the course calls it the Mirage paper.

A **library operating system** (libOS) implements OS services such as the scheduler, device drivers and network stack as ordinary libraries linked into the application. The compiler and linker then produce **one bootable image** that contains the application plus only the OS code it uses, in **one address space** and at **one privilege level**.

blocks.title: The same server as a classic VM and as a unikernel

scenes.caption: A classic VM appliance: the application sits on a full guest OS, which sits on the hypervisor. Most of the user space is never used by nginx.
Two isolation mechanisms are stacked. The hypervisor separates tenants; the guest kernel separates user from kernel inside a VM that holds only one application.
Every send or read pays a trap from user mode into the guest kernel, then the kernel talks to the virtual device.
The unikernel keeps the hypervisor as its only isolation boundary. The OS services become libraries linked next to the application.
Its request path has no trap: a socket call is a plain function call into the network library, which drives the same virtual device.

blocks.md:
Library OSes are an old idea. In the Exokernel design (1995), a tiny kernel did one job: **securely multiplex the hardware**, deciding which application owns which memory pages, disk blocks and network packets. Everything else, even virtual memory and interprocess communication, lived in untrusted library OSes linked into each application. Nemesis (1996) took a similar route. They never caught on, the Mirage paper argues, because each libOS still had to drive real, endlessly varied hardware, with drivers written from scratch or wrapped in a compatibility layer.

The hypervisor removes that problem. It takes over the multiplexing job and presents a small, stable set of **virtual devices** (Xen's netfront and blkfront, the guest halves of its network and block drivers, or virtio on KVM, a standard device interface in which guest and host pass buffers through rings in shared memory), so a unikernel needs only a handful of simple drivers.

What does dropping the general-purpose OS buy? The Mirage DNS appliance compiled to a VM image of **183.5 kB**, while the in-use Linux VM image for BIND, the widely used open-source DNS server, was **462 MB**, about 2,500 times larger. Part of the gap is features (Mirage's DNS server implements less than BIND); much of the rest is code a DNS server never needs: shells, package managers, drivers for hardware the VM will never see.

Unikraft is an open-source toolkit for building unikernels, and its paper at EuroSys 2021 (the European Conference on Computer Systems) reports the same pattern for mainstream software: nginx, SQLite and Redis images of around 1 MB that run in under 10 MB of RAM.
A unikernel is **one application plus only the OS code it uses, linked into one image that boots directly on a hypervisor**. The hypervisor, not a guest kernel, is the isolation boundary.

A unikernel is not a container. A container shares the host's Linux kernel and is isolated by kernel features (namespaces, which give a process its own view of process ids, mounts and network, and cgroups, control groups that cap its CPU, memory and I/O). A unikernel is a real VM with its own tiny kernel, isolated by hardware virtualization.

blocks.question: A team runs exactly one Redis process per VM on a multi-tenant cloud. Which protection does the guest kernel's user/kernel split still provide that the hypervisor does not?
options: It stops other tenants from reading Redis's memory
It is required for the VM to reach the network card
It protects the guest kernel's code and data from a bug or exploit in Redis, inside that one VM
It prevents Redis from being slowed by noisy neighbours
blocks.explain: Tenant isolation and device access come from the hypervisor. The only thing the inner split still buys is protecting the guest kernel from the single application. In a unikernel, a compromised application owns the whole VM, but the VM is all it can reach; this tradeoff comes back in lesson 7.

blocks.question: Why did library operating systems from the 1990s, such as Exokernel, never see wide deployment, while unikernels can run on public clouds?
options: Their libraries were written in unsafe languages
They had to support many kinds of real hardware; a hypervisor exposes a few standard virtual devices instead
They required multicore CPUs that did not exist yet
Hypervisors run library OSes faster than bare metal does
blocks.explain: The Mirage paper's argument: libOSes struggled with real-world hardware support. A hypervisor's virtual devices (netfront, blkfront, virtio) are a small, stable target, so only a few simple drivers are needed.

lessons.title: Syscalls become function calls: one address space, one privilege level

blocks.md:
Recall from the system calls course: a syscall makes the CPU switch from user mode to kernel mode, run kernel entry code and switch back. With KPTI (kernel page-table isolation) it also swaps page tables on every entry and exit. KPTI is the defence against Meltdown, a 2018 CPU flaw that let user code read kernel memory through speculative execution: it keeps kernel memory out of the page tables user code runs with. Such kernel defences against CPU flaws are called **mitigations**, and they add cost to every crossing.

A unikernel has **no user mode at all** for its application. The application, libc and OS libraries share one address space and run at one privilege level, so what used to be a syscall can be an ordinary call instruction.

The Unikraft authors measured a no-op call on an Intel i7-9700K at 3.6 GHz running Linux 5.11 (Table 1 of the paper). At 3.6 GHz one cycle is 1/3.6 ns, so 222 cycles is 222 / 3.6 = 61.67 ns:

- Linux/KVM syscall: **222 cycles** (61.67 ns)
- Linux/KVM syscall, mitigations off: **154 cycles** (42.78 ns)
- Unikraft/KVM syscall through run-time translation: **84 cycles** (23.33 ns)
- A plain function call, on either: **4 cycles** (1.11 ns)

The third row is Unikraft's *binary compatibility* path: an unmodified Linux binary still executes `syscall`, and Unikraft catches and translates it. That is 2.64 times cheaper than Linux with mitigations, but still 21 times the cost of a function call.

blocks.title: Cost of one no-op call (cycles, i7-9700K)

scenes.caption: Linux with its default security mitigations: 222 cycles to enter and leave the kernel for a call that does nothing.
Turning mitigations such as KPTI off saves 68 cycles, but the mode switch itself remains: 154 cycles.
A unikernel running an unmodified binary must still catch each syscall instruction: 84 cycles, cheaper because there is no real privilege change to make.
When the application is linked against the OS libraries, the syscall is a function call: 4 cycles. This is the number unikernels are built to reach.

blocks.md:
How does an unmodified C program end up making function calls? Unikraft ports the **musl** C library (a small, standards-focused libc that suits static linking) and adds a **syscall shim** micro-library. A micro-library is Unikraft's unit of OS code: one small library per component, which lesson 3 covers. Each OS library defines its handlers with a macro, `UK_SYSCALL_R_DEFINE`, which generates a raw handler named after the call (`uk_syscall_r_write` for `write`) plus a libc-style wrapper.

Unikraft's musl port patches musl's internal syscall macro so that it expands, at compile time, to a direct call to that raw handler instead of the `syscall` instruction. Build the application with its own build system, link it into the image, and every `write` or `recvmsg` resolves at link time to the handler. The paper calls this **automatic porting**.

blocks.caption: Excerpts from musl and Unikraft's lib-musl patch 0005. On Linux, write() ends in the syscall instruction; in the unikernel the same source compiles to a direct call to the handler defined below.

blocks.title: Following one write() through each design

scenes.caption: The application code is the same in both worlds. It calls write with file descriptor 1 and a 3 byte buffer.
On Linux, libc loads the syscall number and executes the syscall instruction: a mode switch, entry code and possibly a page table swap. About 222 cycles before any real work.
In Unikraft the shim macro turns the handler into an ordinary C function named after the syscall. The call from libc is a direct jump.
The handler looks up the descriptor in the file descriptor table, the same job the Linux kernel does, but without leaving the address space.
It writes through the open file object and returns the byte count straight to the caller. Simplified: real handlers also take locks when threads are enabled.

blocks.md: How much does this matter for a real server? Model one request as $w$ microseconds of application work plus $k$ syscalls. Only the crossing cost changes between the two designs. On Linux one request takes $w$ plus $k$ crossings at $t_{sys}$ = 61.67 ns each, the 222-cycle measurement. On the unikernel it takes the same $w$ plus $k$ function calls at $t_{call}$ = 1.11 ns each. The speedup $S$ is the old time divided by the new time:

blocks.tex: S = \frac{w + k \cdot t_{\text{sys}}}{w + k \cdot t_{\text{call}}}, \qquad t_{\text{sys}} = 61.67\,\text{ns},\; t_{\text{call}} = 1.11\,\text{ns}
blocks.caption: S is (w + k x 61.67 ns) / (w + k x 1.11 ns). With w = 5 microseconds = 5000 ns and k = 10 syscalls: 10 crossings cost 616.7 ns, 10 calls cost 11.1 ns, so (5000 + 616.7) / (5000 + 11.1) = 1.12, a 12% gain. With w = 1 microsecond the same 10 syscalls give 1.60.

blocks.title: Speedup from removing the syscall crossing

curves.label: Linux no mitigations vs function call

scenes.caption: With 10 syscalls per request, a 5 microsecond request speeds up 1.12 times and a 1 microsecond request 1.60 times. Simplified: counts only the crossing, not cache or TLB effects.
With 50 syscalls and 0.1 microseconds of work, the request is almost all crossing: speedup 20.5. Tiny, I/O-heavy requests gain the most.
With 1 syscall per request the curve is nearly flat: at 10 microseconds of work the gain is 0.6%. Compute-bound code gains almost nothing.

blocks.md:
The model counts only the **direct** cost of a crossing. The system calls course showed a second, **indirect** cost: kernel code evicts your cache lines and TLB entries, and FlexSC measured user code running at reduced speed for up to 14,000 cycles (about 6.1 microseconds at 2.3 GHz) after a single `pwrite`.

Add an indirect cost $p$ per call. Which side pays it? Some pollution may come from the crossing itself (the page-table swap KPTI adds, for one). But much of it comes from OS code simply running, and a unikernel still runs its network stack and filesystem code in the same caches. So the honest model is a range: $p$ on the Linux side only (an upper bound on the gain) or on both sides (a lower bound).

blocks.title: Speedup range once an indirect cost is added

scenes.caption: With p = 0 all three curves coincide: at 5 microseconds of work and 10 syscalls, S = 1.12 as before.

With p = 500 ns per call (an assumed value, not a measurement), the 5 microsecond request could gain 2.12 times if the pollution vanishes, or only 1.06 times if the libOS code pollutes the caches just as much.
With p = 2000 ns the range is 1.02 to 5.11. The direct-only model is neither a floor nor a ceiling; where the truth falls depends on what causes the pollution.

blocks.prompt: Lupine (lesson 9) measured this directly: it ran Linux applications in kernel mode, removing the mode switch but keeping the same kernel code. A null syscall got 40% faster. How much faster do you expect real applications such as nginx and Redis got?
blocks.reveal: **At most 4%.** In Lupine's loop benchmark the 40% gain fell below 5% once only 160 iterations of other work ran between calls. The crossing, plus whatever pollution it alone causes, is a small share of a real request; kernel specialization mattered far more. Treat the speedup model as a rough guide and measure.

blocks.prompt: Unikraft compared nginx and Redis on Unikraft (in a KVM VM) against the same programs running natively on bare-metal Linux, with no hypervisor at all. Which do you expect was faster?
blocks.reveal: Unikraft was **10% to 60% faster than native Linux** in both applications, and 70% to 170% faster than a Linux VM. The authors attribute this to syscall cost (worse with KPTI on) and to linking the mimalloc allocator (a fast general-purpose malloc from Microsoft Research) into the image. A VM is not automatically slower than bare metal when the OS inside it does less work per request.

blocks.md: Unikernel speed comes from **removing the user/kernel crossing**, not from a faster CPU path. Gains are largest for small, syscall-heavy requests and near zero for compute-bound code.

Running an unmodified binary on a unikernel does not get you function-call costs. Trapping and translating each `syscall` cost 84 cycles in Unikraft's measurement, 21 times a function call. Relinking against the libOS is what removes the crossing.

blocks.question: A request handler spends 50 microseconds computing and makes 10 syscalls. Using the model above, roughly how much faster does it get on a unikernel?
options: About 1%
About 12%
About 60%
About 2.6 times
blocks.explain: S = (50000 + 616.7) / (50000 + 11.1) = 1.012, about 1.2%. Removing 600 ns of crossings barely matters next to 50 microseconds of compute.

blocks.question: A team runs an unmodified Linux nginx binary on a unikernel through its binary compatibility layer and sees less gain than the papers report. What is the most likely reason?
options: Binary compatibility disables the hypervisor's virtio drivers
nginx needs fork, which unikernels emulate with slow VM cloning
The binary is compiled for user mode and cannot run in kernel mode
Each syscall instruction still has to be trapped and translated, which costs far more than a direct function call
blocks.explain: The unmodified binary still executes syscall instructions, which the unikernel must catch and dispatch: 84 cycles versus 4 for a direct call in Unikraft's measurement. Linking the application against musl and the syscall shim turns those into direct calls.

lessons.title: Building the image: micro-libraries, configuration and dead code

blocks.md:
A unikernel is specialized **at build time**. Instead of shipping a general OS and configuring it at run time, you pick the OS components your application needs, compile them together with it, and let the compiler and linker throw away everything else.

Unikraft makes this explicit. Every OS component is a **micro-library**: a scheduler, a memory allocator, a network stack, a virtio driver, the boot code. Each has its own Makefile and Kconfig file (the same configuration menu system Linux uses). The build system compiles the selected micro-libraries and links them into one image per target platform.

Micro-libraries that implement the same **API** are interchangeable. Five allocators implement `ukalloc`; cooperative and preemptive schedulers implement `uksched`; lwip (lightweight IP, a small TCP/IP stack written for embedded systems) and others sit on `uknetdev`. An application can also skip a layer entirely: a run-to-completion server, which handles each request fully before taking the next and so never switches between threads, can leave the scheduler out, and a packet processor can call the network driver API without any TCP/IP stack.

blocks.title: Which micro-libraries end up in the image

scenes.caption: The menu of micro-libraries. Nothing is in the image until the configuration or a dependency pulls it in.
Hello world: only platform boot code and nolibc (a tiny Unikraft libc with memcpy and string functions); not even a scheduler or an allocator. The paper reports 200 KB on KVM and 40 KB on Xen.
nginx adds musl, the syscall shim, sockets, a RAM filesystem, a scheduler and the lwip network stack. No block device layer: it only uses ramfs.
A specialized UDP packet server drops the socket layer, lwip and the scheduler, and calls the uknetdev driver API directly in a polling loop.

blocks.md:
Static linking is what makes removal automatic. With every component compiled into one binary, the linker sees the whole program, so **dead code elimination** (DCE: dropping functions and sections nothing references) and **link-time optimization** (LTO: optimizing across what used to be separate libraries) work across the application and the OS together.

Mirage showed the effect in 2013. Its default OCaml build drops unused modules; a dataflow tool called ocamlclean then also drops unused functions inside modules.

blocks.title: Mirage appliance image sizes before and after DCE (MB)

scenes.caption: Standard builds, which already drop unused modules: 0.39 to 0.67 MB including configuration and data.
After function-level dead code elimination: 57% to 74% smaller. The web server shrinks most, from 0.673 to 0.172 MB, 3.9 times smaller.

blocks.md: Configuration moves into the build as well. Mirage compiles configuration files and even data (such as a DNS zone) into the image. That turns misconfiguration into a compile error and lets dead code elimination remove unused features, but it has a cost: to change a setting you rebuild and redeploy. The Mirage paper notes that statically configured VMs can no longer be cloned from one snapshot, and suggests dynamic directives (DHCP, the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, in which a machine asks a server for its IP address at boot, instead of an address fixed in the image) where cloning matters.

blocks.caption: Unikraft's ukalloc front end (lib/ukalloc/include/uk/alloc.h). It is inline, so choosing a backend adds no extra call.

blocks.md: Swapping a component is a configuration change, and the choice matters. With nginx, guest boot time ranged from **0.49 ms with bootalloc** (a simple region allocator) to **3.07 ms with the buddy allocator**, 6.3 times longer. A buddy allocator splits memory into power-of-two blocks, halving a block to fit a small request and merging two free halves (buddies) back together. Other backends include TLSF (two-level segregated fit, a constant-time allocator from real-time systems) and mimalloc. For Redis, the right allocator raised throughput by up to 2.5 times. No single allocator won every workload.

blocks.prompt: For SQLite, Unikraft tried autoporting: build SQLite with its own build system and link the static library into the image, with no source changes. How much slower do you expect it to be than a hand-ported version?
blocks.reveal: Only **1.5% slower** than the manually ported version for 60,000 inserts, and slightly faster than Linux on bare metal. Linking a normal static library into the image already removes the syscall crossings; hand porting adds little on top.

blocks.md: Build-time specialization = **pick components by configuration, link statically, let DCE and LTO remove the rest**. Reconfiguring means rebuilding.

blocks.question: A unikernel serves files only from a RAM filesystem. Why does its image contain no block device driver, even though the Unikraft source tree has one?
options: The hypervisor provides block storage, so the driver is never needed
Block drivers are loaded as kernel modules at boot
Only components selected in the configuration or pulled in as dependencies are compiled and linked; nothing references the block layer
Dead code elimination removes all drivers by default
blocks.explain: Unikraft builds only selected micro-libraries and their dependencies. The paper notes the nginx image has no block subsystem because it only uses RamFS. There are no loadable modules in a unikernel.

blocks.question: A function-as-a-service platform boots a fresh nginx unikernel for each burst of requests and destroys it after a few seconds. Which allocator choice from the Unikraft measurements fits best?
options: A fast-booting allocator such as bootalloc, because boot time dominates a short-lived instance
The buddy allocator, because its throughput at steady state matched TLSF and mimalloc
Any allocator, because allocator choice only affects throughput
mimalloc, because it is always fastest
blocks.explain: For just-in-time instances, boot time matters most, and allocator choice moved nginx guest boot from 0.49 ms (bootalloc) to 3.07 ms (buddy). The paper itself says such a use case should avoid the buddy allocator.

lessons.title: Concurrency in one address space: cooperative threads and no fork

blocks.md:
Three requests arrive at a web server at once. Each needs 1 ms of CPU, then waits 2 ms for a disk or a backend to answer. On Linux you might run a thread per request: when one thread blocks in `read`, the kernel puts it to sleep and runs another. Its scheduler is also **preemptive** (it can stop a running thread at any moment, for example on a timer interrupt), so even a thread that never blocks cannot hold the CPU forever.

A unikernel has one address space, usually one virtual CPU and, in MirageOS, no preemptive threads at all. So who decides what runs while request 1 waits?

MirageOS uses **Lwt**, a concurrency library for OCaml. Its one data type is the *promise*: a value that will be resolved later, such as the bytes a read will return. Code that needs the value waits on it (`let*` in OCaml), and everything after the wait is scheduled to run once the promise resolves. All OCaml code runs in one thread, so there is no locking and no preemption.

This is **cooperative** threading: a handler runs until it reaches a wait, and only then can another run. The Mirage paper puts it plainly: the VM is either executing OCaml code or blocked, with no internal preemption or asynchronous interrupts. On KVM, MirageOS runs on **Solo5**, a thin layer that gives it a few virtual devices and a call, `solo5_yield`, to sleep until I/O arrives or a deadline passes (lesson 5 covers it).

blocks.title: The MirageOS event loop on Solo5 (simplified)

scenes.caption: Each turn of the loop first runs every thread that paused voluntarily or whose timer has expired. Each one runs until it waits again.
If the program's main promise has resolved, the loop ends and the VM exits with that result.
Nothing is runnable. Work out a deadline to sleep until: now if a thread paused, else the next timer, else a day from now.
solo5_yield suspends the whole VM until a network device has input or the deadline passes. The vCPU idles instead of spinning.
The result is a bitmask of up to 64 device handles. Threads waiting on a ready handle are woken, and the loop goes round. Simplified from mirage-solo5 lib/main.ml (hooks omitted, helper renamed).

blocks.title: Three requests on one vCPU (1 ms CPU, 2 ms I/O each)

scenes.caption: One thread, blocking calls: the vCPU sits idle during each wait. Requests finish at 3, 6 and 9 ms (mean 6 ms).
Cooperative event loop: each handler yields when it starts waiting, so the I/O overlaps the next handler. Done at 3, 4 and 5 ms (mean 4 ms), with the same CPU work.
Now R1 computes for 7 ms without ever waiting. Nothing can preempt it, so R2 and R3 cannot even start: all three finish at 9, 10 and 11 ms.

blocks.code:
# 3 requests arrive at t=0. Each: CPU work, then 2 ms of I/O wait.
IO = 2.0

def blocking(cpu):
    t, done = 0.0, []
    for c in cpu:
        t += c + IO        # the only thread sleeps through the I/O
        done.append(t)
    return done

def cooperative(cpu):
    t, done = 0.0, []
    for c in cpu:
        t += c             # handler runs until it waits on I/O
        done.append(t + IO)  # I/O overlaps the next handler
    return done

for name, f, cpu in [("blocking", blocking, [1, 1, 1]),
                     ("cooperative", cooperative, [1, 1, 1]),
                     ("cooperative, R1 7 ms", cooperative, [7, 1, 1])]:
    d = f(cpu)
    print(f"{name:21s} done {d} mean {sum(d)/len(d):.1f} ms")

# Output:
# blocking              done [3.0, 6.0, 9.0] mean 6.0 ms
# cooperative           done [3.0, 4.0, 5.0] mean 4.0 ms
# cooperative, R1 7 ms  done [9.0, 10.0, 11.0] mean 10.0 ms
blocks.caption: The completion times in the figure, computed. Simplified model: no scheduling overhead, all requests arrive at t = 0.

blocks.prompt: A MirageOS handler parses a large request body in one pure OCaml function that runs for 50 ms with no I/O inside. 100 other connections are open. What happens to them during those 50 ms?
blocks.reveal: Nothing happens to them at all. The single vCPU is inside the parser and nothing preempts it, so the event loop never calls `solo5_yield` and no other handler runs: no packets are processed and no timers fire, including the TCP stack's own, which is OCaml code in the same loop. Every connection sees 50 ms of extra latency. The fix is to split the work and call `Lwt.pause ()` between pieces (the loop then sleeps for 0 and runs the others), or move the work to another unikernel.

blocks.md: Cooperative scheduling has no time slices. Any loop that neither waits nor yields holds the only vCPU until it ends, starving every other request and timer in the unikernel.

Unikraft makes scheduling a build-time choice. `uksched` is an API, not a scheduler: the 2021 paper lists cooperative and preemptive schedulers behind it, and the current tree ships `ukschedcoop`, a cooperative round-robin scheduler. Or leave scheduling out: the paper argues an RPC-style server (one that answers each request message, a remote procedure call, with one reply) needs only a single run-to-completion event loop, which removes the scheduler's overhead and the mismatch between the guest's scheduler and the hypervisor's.

With a scheduler, POSIX code such as nginx keeps its threads, and a call that must wait gives the vCPU to another thread.

Why is there no `fork`? `fork` gives the child a copy of the parent's whole address space at the **same virtual addresses**. With one address space and one page table for everything, two copies cannot live at the same addresses.

Unikraft's posix-process library offers three levels. Single thread: `getpid` and friends are stubs, and `clone`, `vfork` and `execve` fail with ENOSYS, the error code for function not implemented. Multithreading: `clone` creates threads. Multiprocess: adds `vfork`, in which the child borrows the parent's memory while the parent waits, and `execve` (optional with threads too) to load another program, which must be built as a position-independent executable (PIE) because everything shares one address space. A copying `fork` is not among them.

blocks.title: Scaling out: one vCPU per unikernel, more unikernels

scenes.caption: One unikernel, one vCPU: every request goes through one event loop, so one core is the ceiling.
To use more cores, start more unikernels and spread connections across them. Each boots in milliseconds and holds only its own state.
State they must share travels over the network, not through shared memory: the Mirage paper's model of multicore as multiple communicating unikernels.

blocks.md: That is how Mirage was designed: one VM per core, with multicore supported via multiple communicating unikernels over one hypervisor. Its web benchmark ran 6 single-vCPU Mirage unikernels against Apache2 (the Apache HTTP Server, a widely used web server) in a Linux VM with 6 vCPUs, in 2 VMs with 3 vCPUs each, and in 6 VMs with 1 vCPU each. Scaling out helped Apache2 more than adding cores, and the unikernels beat Apache2 in every configuration.

A unikernel runs many requests on one vCPU by **interleaving at waits**: an event loop or cooperative threads overlap I/O, a long computation blocks everyone, and more cores means **more unikernels**, not more threads.

blocks.question: Four requests arrive together at a single-vCPU cooperative event loop. Each needs 2 ms of CPU and then 3 ms of I/O wait. When does the last one finish?
options: At 8 ms, when the last handler stops computing
At 11 ms
At 20 ms, since each request takes 5 ms
At 5 ms, since all four overlap fully
blocks.explain: CPU work cannot overlap on one vCPU: handlers run at 0-2, 2-4, 4-6 and 6-8 ms. Each I/O overlaps the next handler, so the last request waits from 8 to 11 ms. A blocking single thread would take 4 x 5 = 20 ms.

blocks.question: A service forks a worker process per connection. A team wants to run it on Unikraft with the multiprocess option of posix-process enabled. What should they expect?
options: fork works, since the multiprocess level emulates it with copy-on-write pages
fork works, but each child gets its own VM
The service runs unchanged if it is built as PIE
There is no copying fork; they need a thread-based mode or a redesign, since vfork only borrows the parent's memory until execve or exit
blocks.explain: One address space cannot hold a second copy at the same addresses. posix-process offers vfork plus execve (of PIE programs) at its multiprocess level, which suits launching another program, not cloning a worker. Many servers can run as one process instead: the Unikraft catalog runs nginx with `master_process off` and one worker.

lessons.title: Booting on the hypervisor: virtual devices, boot time and memory

blocks.md:
A unikernel boots as a normal VM. A **virtual machine monitor** (VMM: the user-space program that creates the VM, such as QEMU or Firecracker on KVM) loads the image into guest memory and starts the virtual CPU at its entry point. QEMU is the general-purpose open-source emulator that can model many devices and firmware; Firecracker is Amazon's minimal VMM, built for AWS Lambda, that offers only a few virtio devices. From there the unikernel's own boot code sets up memory and drivers and calls the application's `main`.

There is no init system, no root filesystem to mount, no services to start. The boot path does only what the selected libraries need.

blocks.title: From VMM start to the first request

scenes.caption: The VMM creates the VM, copies the image into guest memory and starts the virtual CPU at the image's entry point.
Unikraft's default image carries a pre-built page table. Boot code just enables paging and points the CPU at it: about 30 microseconds for 1 GB of memory.
The boot code hands the heap to the configured allocator, then initializes only the drivers in the image, such as virtio-net.
Then it calls main. The guest part of boot, from first instruction to main, took tens to hundreds of microseconds on QEMU and Solo5.
From now on, a send is a function call into the network library, which places the packet on the virtio ring and notifies the host.

blocks.md:
The device interface a unikernel needs is small. Solo5, the sandboxed execution environment that runs MirageOS on KVM and other hosts, exposes a small guest API: acquire, read and write for a network device and for a block device, a monotonic and a wall clock, a console write, `solo5_yield` to sleep until I/O is ready or a deadline passes, thread-local storage setup, and exit. Everything above that (TCP/IP, filesystems, TLS) is library code inside the unikernel.

On Xen, Mirage's drivers speak the split-driver protocol: a shared memory page of request slots with producer and consumer indices, plus an event channel to signal the other side. The next lesson draws both kinds of ring.

Because the guest does so little, **the VMM dominates boot time**. For a hello world on Unikraft, total boot (VMM plus guest) was about 3 ms on Firecracker and Solo5, about 10 ms with QEMU's microVM machine type (a stripped-down QEMU configuration with few devices, inspired by Firecracker) and about 40 ms with standard QEMU. The guest's own share was under 1 ms in every case.

blocks.title: Where boot time goes (hello world on Unikraft)

scenes.caption: Lightweight VMMs set up a VM in a few milliseconds. The guest share (green) is at most 1 ms. Simplified: totals rounded from the paper, guest shares are upper bounds.
Heavier VMMs emulate more devices and firmware. QEMU microVM reaches about 10 ms and standard QEMU about 40 ms, with the same tiny guest share.
The lesson: once the guest is a unikernel, shaving the guest further barely moves total boot. Pick a lightweight VMM.

blocks.md: Guest boot time is where the OS design shows. In the comparison below, OSv, Rump and HermiTux are other unikernels, uHyve is HermiTux's own minimal hypervisor, and Alpine is a small general-purpose Linux distribution. The Unikraft paper lists guest boot times reported for other systems: MirageOS 1 to 2 ms on Solo5, OSv 4 to 5 ms on Firecracker, Rump 14 to 15 ms on Solo5, HermiTux 30 to 32 ms on uHyve, Lupine (a specialized Linux) 70 ms on Firecracker, and an Alpine Linux VM about 330 ms on Firecracker.

blocks.title: Guest boot time by OS (upper end of reported range, ms)

scenes.caption: A general-purpose Linux guest takes about 330 ms to boot. Every specialized system is at least 4.7 times faster.
Among unikernels, the ones that initialize least boot fastest: Unikraft under 1 ms and MirageOS 2 ms. Rough comparison only: the VMMs differ.

blocks.md: Memory follows the same logic. Unikraft guests needed only **2 to 6 MB** of RAM to boot nginx, Redis, SQLite or hello world. Mirage's web appliance ran in 32 MB against 256 MB for the Linux VM it was compared with. Small footprints mean more VMs per host, and fast boots mean VMs can be started per request instead of kept warm.

How does memory work inside? There is one address space and one page table, set up at boot. The heap is simply the memory the VMM gave the VM. Solo5 hands the application one contiguous, non-executable read/write region and its size, used for both heap and stacks. Unikraft's boot code gives all free guest memory, minus the pages its page tables need, to the configured allocator.

Nothing is swapped to disk: neither Solo5's guest API nor Unikraft's library tree has a swap layer. Unikraft can optionally add demand paging (its `ukvmem` library maps a heap page only when it is first touched), but those pages still come from the VM's own memory.

When the heap runs out, an allocation simply fails: `uk_malloc` returns NULL (the allocator front end in lesson 3). There is no other process to kill and no disk to page to. So you size the VM for the application's peak heap: `kraft run` (Unikraft's command-line tool, lesson 8) gives 64 MiB unless you pass `-M`, and Mirage's tutorial shows Solo5 reporting 512 MB addressable with heap and stack sharing one region. Lesson 8 reads that memory map.

blocks.title: Mirage's sealing: no page writable and executable

scenes.caption: At start of day, before sealing, nothing stops a page from being both writable and executable.
The unikernel builds page tables in which code is read and execute only and every writable page is non-executable (W xor X).
It then issues a seal hypercall. The hypervisor refuses later page table changes, so injected code can never become executable. I/O mappings stay allowed if non-executable.
An exploit that writes code into the heap and tries to mark it executable fails: the hypervisor rejects the page table change. The cost is a fixed heap size from boot.

blocks.md: Mirage also randomizes addresses **at compile time**: since reconfiguring means relinking anyway, each build can use a freshly generated linker script, instead of shipping a runtime loader for address space layout randomization (ASLR: placing code, heap and stack at unpredictable addresses so an exploit cannot know where to jump). Sealing needed a hypervisor patch of under 50 lines to Xen 4.1; without it Mirage still runs, minus that defence.

Do not assume every unikernel does this. Sealing and compile-time randomization are Mirage's design; a 2019 study by the security firm NCC Group of two other unikernels, Rumprun and IncludeOS, found ASLR, W xor X and stack canaries (a random value placed before a function's return address and checked on return, so a buffer overflow is caught) absent or broken.

blocks.question: A unikernel's guest boot takes 0.3 ms and total VM start takes 40 ms on standard QEMU. What will most reduce cold-start latency?
options: Removing more micro-libraries from the image
Using a faster memory allocator
Moving from KVM to emulation mode
Switching to a lightweight VMM such as Firecracker or Solo5
blocks.explain: The guest is under 1% of the 40 ms. Unikraft's measurements put total boot at about 3 ms on Firecracker and Solo5 versus about 40 ms on QEMU, so the VMM choice is the lever.

blocks.question: Mirage seals a unikernel so no page table changes are allowed after start of day. Which consequence must the application live with?
options: It cannot receive network packets
It must pre-allocate all the memory it needs at startup, since the heap cannot grow by mapping new pages
It cannot use a garbage collector
It must run with a single vCPU
blocks.explain: The paper states a sealed VM cannot expand its heap and must pre-allocate its memory at boot; allocation within the heap and I/O mappings still work. The single vCPU in Mirage is a separate design choice, not a consequence of sealing.

lessons.title: Paravirtual I/O up close: one packet through a virtqueue

blocks.md:
Every unikernel in this course reaches the outside world the same way: it writes buffers into memory it shares with the hypervisor and then rings a doorbell. Lesson 5 said a send places the packet on the virtio ring and notifies the host. This lesson opens the ring.

The tiny example: the guest sends two Ethernet frames, a 98-byte ping and a full-size 1514-byte frame, through a queue with 8 slots. The **driver** is the guest's code (here the unikernel's virtio-net driver); the **device** is the host side that emulates the network card.

A **virtqueue** is virtio's queue of buffers. The *split* format has three parts in guest memory, each written by only one side:

- **Descriptor table** (driver writes): 16 bytes per entry. `addr` is the guest-physical address of a buffer, `len` its length, `flags` has NEXT (1, the buffer continues in entry `next`) and WRITE (2, the device may write into it).
- **Available ring** (driver writes): `flags`, `idx`, and `ring[]`, the head descriptor of each buffer chain offered to the device.
- **Used ring** (device writes): `flags`, `idx`, and `ring[]` of (id, len) pairs for finished chains.

Both `idx` fields are free-running counters: the slot is `idx` modulo the queue size, which is always a power of 2.

blocks.title: Sending two frames through an 8-slot split virtqueue

scenes.caption: Empty queue. Both counters start at 0: avail.idx is where the driver puts its next entry, used.idx where the device puts its next.
Frame 1: the driver fills descriptor 0 with the 12-byte virtio-net header (per-packet metadata such as offload hints) (flag NEXT, next = 1) and descriptor 1 with the 98-byte frame (end of chain).
It publishes the chain by writing its head, 0, into avail.ring[0] and bumping avail.idx to 1. Then it kicks the device: on KVM, a VM exit, where the vCPU stops and the host takes over.
Frame 2 uses descriptors 2 and 3 (header, then 1514 bytes) and avail.ring[1] = 2, so avail.idx = 2. If the device has said it is busy, no second kick is needed.
The device sends both frames and returns the chain heads in the used ring as (id, len): (0, 0) and (2, 0). used.idx reaches 2, and it may raise one interrupt for both.
The driver sees used.idx moved, frees descriptors 0 to 3 for reuse, and the counters keep counting up. Simplified: real drivers keep a free list and may use one descriptor per frame.

blocks.prompt: The device has sent both frames. What `len` does it write into each used ring entry?
blocks.reveal: **0.** The used ring's `len` counts the bytes the device *wrote* into the device-writable part of the chain. A transmit chain is all device-readable (no WRITE flag), so nothing was written. On the receive queue the same field tells the driver how many bytes of a frame arrived.

blocks.code:
QSIZE, NEXT = 8, 1                 # queue size 8; flag NEXT = 1
desc = [None] * QSIZE              # (len, flags, next)
avail_ring, used_ring = [None] * QSIZE, [None] * QSIZE
avail_idx = used_idx = 0
free = list(range(QSIZE))

def send(frame_len):               # driver side
    global avail_idx
    h, d = free.pop(0), free.pop(0)
    desc[h] = (12, NEXT, d)        # 12-byte virtio-net header
    desc[d] = (frame_len, 0, 0)    # the frame, end of chain
    avail_ring[avail_idx % QSIZE] = h
    avail_idx += 1                 # free-running counter

def device():                      # host side
    global used_idx
    while used_idx < avail_idx:
        head = avail_ring[used_idx % QSIZE]
        used_ring[used_idx % QSIZE] = (head, 0)  # wrote 0 bytes
        used_idx += 1

for f in (98, 1514):
    send(f)
    print("after", f, "byte frame: avail_idx", avail_idx)
print("desc", desc[:4])
device()
print("used", used_ring[:2], "used_idx", used_idx)

# Output:
# after 98 byte frame: avail_idx 1
# after 1514 byte frame: avail_idx 2
# desc [(12, 1, 1), (98, 0, 0), (12, 1, 3), (1514, 0, 0)]
# used [(0, 0), (2, 0)] used_idx 2
blocks.caption: The same two sends as a model of the split ring, run to produce the values in the figure. Real drivers also add memory barriers between filling a descriptor and bumping idx.

blocks.md: Notice that moving data needs no exits: both sides just read and write shared memory. The expensive part is the **notification**. On KVM, the driver's kick is a write to a device register that stops the guest's vCPU and returns control to the host, a **VM exit**; the notification back is an interrupt injected into the guest (Red Hat's [virtio overview](https://www.redhat.com/en/blog/virtio-devices-and-drivers-overview-headjack-and-phone) walks through this path). So the cost to count is notifications per packet, not bytes.

Both sides can say do not disturb. The device can set `VIRTQ_USED_F_NO_NOTIFY` in the used ring's flags, for example while it is already working through buffers, and the driver sets `VIRTQ_AVAIL_F_NO_INTERRUPT` when it does not want interrupts. With the `VIRTIO_F_EVENT_IDX` feature each side instead publishes an index (`avail_event`, `used_event`) meaning: notify me only when you place an entry at that index. The spec calls these hints, not synchronized with the other side, so both must handle spurious notifications.

blocks.title: Driver kicks (VM exits) to send 4 frames

scenes.caption: Kick after every frame: 4 frames cost 4 VM exits, each far more expensive than writing a 16-byte descriptor.
Add all 4 frames, bump avail.idx once, kick once: 1 exit for the batch. This is why APIs take arrays of packets.
If the device is busy polling the ring and has set NO_NOTIFY, the driver skips the kick entirely: 0 exits. Simplified: the host spends a core polling instead.

blocks.md: This explains lesson 7's fastest result. Unikraft's `uknetdev` API takes arrays of packets (`uk_netdev_tx_burst`, `uk_netdev_rx_burst`) and by default runs a queue in **polling mode**: the application calls the receive function in a loop, which checks the ring itself, so it never waits for an interrupt. An application can switch a queue to interrupt mode, in which the interrupt line is enabled only when there is no more work. The paper also notes the host side can poll (vhost-user, a virtio transport running in host user space) at the cost of polling in the host. The key-value store that reached 6.3 million requests per second coded against this API in polling mode.

Xen's split drivers use the same idea with one ring. The guest's frontend (netfront) and a backend driver in another domain (Xen's name for a VM; the backend usually runs in the privileged dom0) share one memory page divided into fixed-size slots. The frontend writes requests and advances `req_prod`; the backend writes responses into the same slots and advances `rsp_prod`; each side keeps its own consumer index. An **event channel**, Xen's virtual interrupt line, signals the other side, and `req_event` and `rsp_event` play the role of virtio's event indices: notify only when the producer passes them. Data pages are shared by granting the other domain access through the hypervisor.

blocks.title: Notifications for a batch, with and without suppression

scenes.caption: The driver writes descriptors and the available ring: plain memory writes, no exit.
The device's notifications are enabled, so the driver kicks: one VM exit.
The device sets NO_NOTIFY and starts draining the ring.
More frames arrive from the guest while the device is busy. The driver reads the flag and skips the kick.
The device returns all four in the used ring and sends one interrupt, unless the driver suppressed that too.

blocks.md: A virtqueue is **three shared arrays and two counters**. Data moves through memory for free; only **notifications** cost VM exits and interrupts, so batching, suppression and polling set the price of each packet.

blocks.question: With VIRTIO_F_EVENT_IDX negotiated, the device has set avail_event = 5. The driver adds buffers one at a time, taking the available ring's idx from 3 up to 7. After which addition must it notify?
options: After every addition, since notifications are never optional
When idx becomes 5
When idx goes from 5 to 6: the entry was placed at index 5
Never, because event indices replace notifications
blocks.explain: The spec says the driver must notify when the idx that determined where the new entry went equals avail_event, that is when idx reaches avail_event + 1 = 6. Other additions should not notify.

blocks.question: Why does a unikernel coded against uknetdev in polling mode handle millions of packets per second where an interrupt-per-packet design does not?
options: It checks the ring in a loop and moves packets in bursts, so it pays no interrupt or notification per packet
Polling makes each descriptor smaller
Polling lets the guest write directly to the physical network card
Polling disables the hypervisor's isolation
blocks.explain: The ring itself is just memory. Per-packet costs come from notifications: interrupts into the guest and kicks out of it. Polling and burst APIs remove them from the hot path, at the price of a core that spins.

lessons.title: Specializing further, and what you give up

blocks.md:
Removing syscalls helps unmodified applications. The bigger wins come when an application is **rewritten against lower-level APIs** that a general-purpose OS cannot expose without breaking its own layering.

The Unikraft authors built a UDP key-value store, one request per packet, and ran it several ways. The basic version uses `recvmsg` and `sendmsg`, one packet per call. Batching (`recvmmsg`/`sendmmsg`) amortizes the syscalls. Porting to DPDK (the Data Plane Development Kit, a kernel bypass framework: the application polls the network card directly from user space) removes the kernel from the data path entirely.

blocks.title: UDP key-value store throughput (thousand requests/s)

scenes.caption: Socket APIs everywhere: one syscall per packet. Batching adds about 50% (418 to 627 K/s in the guest), but all of these stay near a million or below.
Note the Unikraft lwip version: 319 K/s, below the Linux guest. Removing syscalls does not help if the network stack itself is slower.
Coding against the driver API changes the scale: DPDK in a Linux guest reaches 6.4 M/s and Unikraft's uknetdev in polling mode 6.3 M/s, 19.7 times its lwip version.

blocks.md: Throughput alone says the two fast versions tie. The resources differ: the DPDK guest used **two cores** (one dedicated to DPDK), about 1 GB of image and a boot of a few seconds. The Unikraft version used **one core**, a 1.4 MB image and booted in 80 ms. Per core, that is 3.2 versus 6.3 million requests per second. Both needed a similar porting effort, since both mean rewriting the network path.

blocks.prompt: Given those numbers, would you expect a Unikraft image running unmodified nginx with its lwip stack to beat Linux on raw packet processing in general?
blocks.reveal: Not necessarily. The key-value store showed lwip on Unikraft at 319 K/s, **below** the Linux guest's 418 K/s with sockets. The nginx and Redis gains came from syscall savings and allocator choice, not a faster TCP/IP stack. Linux's network stack is heavily tuned; a unikernel's stack may not be. Measure your workload.

blocks.md:
Now the costs. The papers and later studies agree on four.

1. **Security hardening may be missing.** The NCC Group study (2019) found ASLR, W xor X, stack canaries and heap integrity checks absent or flawed in Rumprun and IncludeOS. Worse, with no privilege split, code execution in the application *is* code execution in the kernel: an attacker can immediately do things like arbitrary packet I/O that would need privilege escalation on Linux.
2. **Compatibility is partial.** POSIX (the Portable Operating System Interface) is the standard Unix API that Linux software expects. Unikraft's docs report 160+ Linux syscalls implemented; missing ones are stubbed and return ENOSYS (lesson 4). Everything shares one address space, so a copying `fork` is impossible. The 2021 paper supported no processes at all; current Unikraft adds optional `vfork` and `execve` (posix-process), but software built around `fork` still needs a thread-based mode or changes.

3. **Debugging and operations change.** There is no shell to log into, no `ps`, no `strace` inside the VM. Unikraft offers gdb support (attached to the VM through QEMU's gdb stub) and a ukdebug library with trace points; its `linuxu` user-space target, used for development at the time of the paper, was retired in 2024. Mirage similarly develops on a Unix target first and builds for a hypervisor target (Solo5 hvt or Xen) last.
4. **Scaling is per VM.** Mirage runs one vCPU per unikernel and scales by running more unikernels; Unikraft's paper evaluated single-core images and listed multi-core support as work in progress. Check the current project docs before assuming SMP (symmetric multiprocessing: one kernel running on several cores that share memory).

blocks.title: Choosing a deployment model for one service

nodes.label:
Need many processes,
fork, or a shell?

Cold start, density or
attack surface matter?

Hot path needs more
than syscall savings?

scenes.caption: First filter: a unikernel runs one program, with at most limited process support. Software built around fork, many cooperating processes or interactive shells belongs in a Linux VM or container.
If nothing pushes you to millisecond boots, high density or a minimal attack surface, a container gives most of the convenience with familiar tools.
Otherwise link the application into a unikernel. If the hot path is bound by the stack itself, rewrite it against the low-level API, as with the key-value store.

blocks.md: Unikernels trade **generality for specialization**: fewer layers, smaller images, faster boots and cheaper calls, paid for with porting work, partial POSIX, no processes, weaker tooling and security that depends entirely on what the libOS implements.

MirageOS's answer to the security cost is language safety: its whole stack, TCP/IP included, is OCaml. The paper notes that of 40 BIND vulnerabilities over 10 years, 25% were memory management errors, 15% poor handling of exceptional data and 10% faulty parsing, all of which type safety would mitigate. That is 20 of the 40.

blocks.question: An attacker finds a buffer overflow in a C web server. On a Linux VM they get code execution as the unprivileged web server user. What changes if the same server runs as a unikernel without memory protections?
options: They get code execution with full control of the VM, including raw packet I/O, with no privilege escalation step needed
Nothing: the hypervisor stops the exploit before it runs
The exploit fails because unikernels have no shell to spawn
They can immediately read the memory of other VMs on the host
blocks.explain: With one address space and one privilege level, the application is the kernel. NCC Group showed arbitrary packet I/O right after compromise. The hypervisor still confines the attacker to that VM, so other tenants remain protected unless the hypervisor itself is broken.

blocks.question: A team ports a UDP service to a unikernel using the standard socket API on lwip, and it is slower than on a Linux VM. Which next step matches the evidence from the Unikraft key-value experiment?
options: Enable binary compatibility to use Linux's network stack
Add more vCPUs, since lwip scales linearly
Code the hot path against the uknetdev driver API in polling mode, bypassing the TCP/IP stack and sockets
Switch the allocator to buddy for better throughput
blocks.explain: lwip sockets gave 319 K/s; coding against uknetdev gave 6.3 M/s on one core. Binary compatibility does not bring Linux's network stack into the unikernel, and the evaluated images were single-core.

blocks.question: Which service is the weakest candidate for a unikernel?
options: A stateless HTTP API that must cold-start in milliseconds per request burst
A DNS server facing the internet where attack surface matters
A UDP packet processor that needs millions of packets per second per core
A CI build runner that shells out to compilers, git and test scripts in many child processes
blocks.explain: The build runner depends on fork, exec and many separate programs, which a single-address-space unikernel supports poorly at best: there is no copying fork, and Unikraft's vfork plus execve covers only simple spawning. The other three match unikernel strengths: fast boot, small attack surface and low-level I/O specialization.

lessons.title: Hands-on: build, boot and measure a unikernel

blocks.md:
Every number so far came from papers. This lesson walks the real toolchains so you can reproduce them. The commands come from the official docs and need a host with hardware virtualization: Linux with KVM for Unikraft's `kraft`, and Linux, FreeBSD or OpenBSD for Mirage's Solo5 `hvt` target.

Outputs marked *published* are copied from the projects' documentation. They were **not run here**: the machine that wrote this course has no KVM. Run them yourself and compare.

`kraft` is Unikraft's command-line tool. A project is described by a **Kraftfile**: which Unikraft version, which libraries, which Kconfig options, and which **targets**, platform and architecture pairs such as `qemu/x86_64` or `fc/x86_64` (fc is Firecracker). `kraft build` produces one image per target, and `kraft run` boots it. Today `kraft run` drives KVM guests only, through QEMU or Firecracker; without hardware virtualization QEMU falls back to emulation, which the docs warn is much slower.

blocks.code:
# Install kraft (from the Unikraft catalog README)
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://get.kraftkit.sh | sh

# 1. C hello world from the catalog: build and boot
git clone https://github.com/unikraft/catalog
cd catalog/examples/helloworld-gcc13.2
kraft run --rm --plat qemu --arch x86_64 .
kraft run --rm --plat qemu --arch x86_64 -M 256M .   # more memory

# 2. nginx as a prebuilt image, host port 8080 to guest port 80
kraft run -p 8080:80 unikraft.org/nginx:1.25
curl localhost:8080

# 3. List instances: name, source, state, memory, platform
kraft ps
blocks.caption: From the Unikraft catalog READMEs and the kraft running guide. Not run here (no KVM on this machine).

blocks.md: The docs' published `kraft ps` output shows instances with `MEM 64M` on `qemu/x86_64`: 64 MiB is `kraft run`'s default memory. Now open the catalog's nginx Kraftfile. It does not compile nginx from source. It uses `app-elfloader`, a Unikraft application that loads an unmodified Linux ELF binary, and turns on `CONFIG_LIBSYSCALL_SHIM_HANDLER`, the handler for real `syscall` instructions. It also enables `ukvmem` and link-time optimization with dead code elimination (`CONFIG_OPTIMIZE_LTO`, `CONFIG_OPTIMIZE_DEADELIM`).

blocks.prompt: Given that Kraftfile, which per-call cost from lesson 2 should you expect each nginx system call to pay?
blocks.reveal: The **trapped** path: about 84 cycles per call in Unikraft's measurement, not the 4-cycle function call. A binary-compatible image catches each `syscall` instruction and dispatches it. That is the convenient way to run nginx today; relinking nginx against musl and the syscall shim, as the paper did, is what turns calls into direct jumps. The same machinery gives you a debugging aid: the docs offer an strace-like loader, `kraft run --elfloader loaders.unikraft.org/strace:latest BINARY`.

blocks.md: MirageOS separates *what* the unikernel needs from *where* it runs. `config.ml` declares the devices (a clock, a network, a block device); `mirage configure -t unix` builds the program as an ordinary Unix process, which you debug with the usual tools (on macOS the target is `-t macosx`). `mirage configure -t hvt` builds the same code for Solo5's hvt **tender**: a small host program that loads the unikernel into a hardware-virtualized VM, attaches host devices to it and runs it.

blocks.code:
git clone https://github.com/mirage/mirage-skeleton.git
cd mirage-skeleton/tutorial/hello
mirage configure -t unix && make depends && dune build
dist/hello                      # an ordinary process

mirage configure -t hvt && make depends && dune build
solo5-hvt dist/hello.hvt        # the same code as a VM

# Published output (MirageOS hello-world tutorial):
# Solo5: Memory map: 512 MB addressable:
# Solo5:   unused @ (0x0 - 0xfffff)
# Solo5:     text @ (0x100000 - 0x1e8fff)
# Solo5:   rodata @ (0x1e9000 - 0x220fff)
# Solo5:     data @ (0x221000 - 0x2d0fff)
# Solo5:     heap >= 0x2d1000 < stack < 0x20000000
# ... INF [application] hello   (four times, a second apart)
# Solo5: solo5_exit(0) called
blocks.caption: Commands from the MirageOS hello-world tutorial; the Solo5 lines are the tutorial's published output. Not run here.

blocks.title: Reading Solo5's memory map

scenes.caption: The VM has 512 MB of addressable memory. The first 1 MiB is left unused.
The image itself: code, read-only data and data. 0x100000 to 0x2d0fff is 1860 KiB, about 1.8 MiB for this hello world.
Everything else, about 509 MiB, is one region shared by the heap (growing up) and the stack (growing down). Give the VM less memory and this region shrinks; there is no swap behind it.

blocks.md:
Now measure boot the way the papers do, splitting it in two. Unikraft's paper timed the VMM separately from the guest, whose share runs from the first guest instruction until `main` is called. Firecracker's paper timed from forking the VMM process until the guest wrote to a special I/O port.

On your machine: total time is the wall clock from launching the VMM to the application's first output, and the guest share needs a timestamp from inside the guest, as the papers added (Firecracker's had the guest write to an I/O port, and the VMM was modified to exit on that write). Time a second run too: on first use, `kraft run` downloads an image it does not have yet.

What should you see? Published results: for a Unikraft hello world, about 3 ms total on Firecracker and Solo5, about 10 ms on QEMU's microVM machine type and about 40 ms on standard QEMU, with the guest's share under 1 ms everywhere. Firecracker with a minimal Linux guest boots to application code in under 125 ms. Your numbers will differ with CPU, host kernel and VMM version; check the shape, that the VMM dominates, rather than the decimals.

blocks.code:
# Lesson 2 model: S = (w + k*t_sys) / (w + k*t_call). Solve for w given a measured S.
T_SYS, T_CALL = 61.67, 1.11        # ns per crossing / per call (Unikraft Table 1)

def work_needed(S, k):
    return k * (T_SYS - S * T_CALL) / (S - 1)

for S in (1.7, 2.7):               # Unikraft nginx: 70% to 170% faster than a Linux VM
    for k in (10, 50):
        print(f"S={S} k={k:2d}: w = {work_needed(S, k):6.0f} ns")

# Output:
# S=1.7 k=10: w =    854 ns

blocks.caption: Can lesson 2's model explain Unikraft's measured nginx gain over a Linux VM? Solve the model for the work per request it would require.

blocks.md: The model needs under 1 microsecond of application work per request (at 10 syscalls) to produce a 1.7 times speedup from crossings alone, and less for 2.7. That is very little work for an HTTP request, and the paper itself credits both the syscall savings and the mimalloc allocator. To test the model on your own service: count syscalls per request on Linux (for example with `strace -c` over a known number of requests), measure requests per second on both platforms with the same load generator, and compare the measured ratio with the model's prediction.

Develop on a hosted target where one exists. Mirage's `-t unix` builds the same code as a normal Unix program, where gdb, perf and strace all work; switch to `hvt` only once it runs. Unikraft retired its `linuxu` user-space target in 2024, so there you attach gdb to the VM itself through QEMU's gdb stub.

blocks.question: You time `kraft run unikraft.org/nginx:1.25` for the first time on a fresh machine and it takes several seconds. Before blaming the VMM, what should you rule out?
options: That nginx is compiled with a slow allocator
That the VM has too much memory
That lwip needs seconds to negotiate DHCP on every boot
That kraft spent the time downloading the OCI image (the standard container image format kraft packages unikernels in), which it does on first use; time a second run
blocks.explain: The kraft docs say an OCI image not present on the host is downloaded before it is executed. A fair boot measurement excludes that, and separates the VMM's share from the guest's.

blocks.question: Your Mirage unikernel crashes inside its HTTP handler and you want a debugger and a profiler. Which target do you build?
options: hvt, because only the VM build has the real network stack
unix (or macosx), because the same code then runs as an ordinary process
virtio, because it has the most devices
None: unikernels cannot be debugged
blocks.explain: Mirage builds the same application against different device implementations. The Unix target produces a normal executable, so ordinary debuggers and profilers work; you switch to hvt for deployment.

lessons.title: The spectrum: Linux-based unikernels, microVMs and sandboxes

blocks.md: Lesson 2 credited unikernel speed to removing the user/kernel crossing; lesson 3 credited small images to build-time specialization. Which one matters more? Several projects tested this by moving Linux itself toward unikernel properties. Together with microVMs and sandboxes, they fill the space between a full Linux VM and a unikernel, and a real choice usually lands somewhere in that space.

**OSv** (USENIX ATC 2014) is a guest OS for running one existing Linux application per VM. The kernel, written in C++11, and all threads share one address space. Its kernel contains an ELF dynamic linker that loads ordinary dynamically linked Linux programs and resolves their calls to functions glibc normally provides, `read()` included, to OSv's own implementations, so those calls are plain function calls. OSv supports SMP VMs; `fork()` and `exec()` are not provided. The paper reports Memcached booted and serving in 0.6 s from an 11 MB image, and up to 25% more throughput and 47% less latency for unmodified network-heavy applications.

**Lupine Linux** (EuroSys 2020) asks how close plain Linux can get, using two unikernel techniques. **Specialization** uses Kconfig to drop drivers, multiprocessing support and anything the application does not need. **Kernel Mode Linux** (KML), an out-of-tree patch, runs the application in kernel mode so a system call needs no mode switch.

Against Firecracker's recommended microVM kernel, Lupine reached a 4 MB image, a 23 ms boot (measured without KML; see below), a 21 MB memory footprint and up to 33% more throughput. Because it is Linux, an application that calls `fork` keeps working, where many unikernels crash.

blocks.title: What removing the mode switch bought Lupine (KML gain, %)

scenes.caption: KML cut the latency of a null system call by 40%: the crossing really is cheaper.
Add a little work between calls and the gain fades fast: with 160 loop iterations it is already below 5% (shown at that bound).
On real applications KML added at most 4%. Lupine's gains came mostly from specialization, and its authors conclude syscall overhead should not be a primary concern.

blocks.md:
KML had a second cost. It is incompatible with `CONFIG_PARAVIRT`, the option that lets Linux replace some privileged hardware operations with cheaper calls to the hypervisor, and a primary enabler of fast Linux boots; without it Lupine's boot rose to 71 ms. That is why the Unikraft paper lists Lupine at 70 ms with KML and 18 ms without.

**Unikernel Linux** (UKL, EuroSys 2023, Boston University and Red Hat) goes further. A Linux configuration option links one application with the kernel into one image that runs at supervisor privilege, after only a re-link against a slightly modified kernel and glibc. Unmodified applications gain modestly; deeper changes, such as calling internal kernel routines directly, gave Redis 26% more throughput. UKL keeps multi-core execution, runs on bare metal and in VMs, and lets ordinary processes run beside the UKL process and talk to it over standard IPC (interprocess communication, such as pipes and sockets). The kernel changes are about 1,250 lines.

Two neighbours are not unikernels at all.

- **Firecracker** (NSDI 2020) is a minimal VMM, about 50,000 lines of Rust, running a normal minimally configured Linux guest. With its minimal Linux guest configuration it boots to application code in under 125 ms, adds under 5 MB of memory per microVM and can create up to 150 microVMs per second per host. Inside you keep full Linux: `fork`, `strace`, shells.
- **gVisor** is an application kernel written in Go that runs in user space. It intercepts a container's system calls and implements them itself, adding seccomp rules on the host as defence in depth. It keeps the container's process-like resource model, at the price of reduced compatibility and higher per-syscall overhead.

blocks.title: From full Linux to a pure unikernel

scenes.caption: Isolation boundary: gVisor sandboxes on the host kernel; everything else is a VM behind a hypervisor (UKL can also run on bare metal, dashed).
Linux behaviour inside, with many processes and familiar tools: Firecracker with Linux, Lupine and UKL (UKL's linked application itself gets only a modified fork).
No mode switch for the application's kernel calls: Lupine (via KML), UKL, OSv, Unikraft relinked and MirageOS.
Smallest images and fastest boots, at the price of partial POSIX or a single language: the libOS unikernels on the right.

blocks.title: Boot time as each paper reports it (ms)

scenes.caption: Upper ends of reported values: Unikraft hello world about 3 ms total, MirageOS guest 2 ms, Lupine 23 ms without KML (71 ms with it), a minimal Linux guest on Firecracker under 125 ms end to end.
Read the shape, not the decimals: different years, machines, and start and stop points (guest only versus VMM plus guest).

blocks.md: These systems were measured in different papers, on different hardware, with different definitions of boot. OSv's 0.6 s, for example, used its ZFS filesystem; Lupine's authors found a read-only filesystem made OSv boot 10 times faster. Compare within one paper, or measure yourself.

Unikernel gains split into **removing the crossing** (small for real applications, per Lupine) and **specializing** (large). Linux can deliver much of the second. Choose a libOS unikernel when you also want tiny images, millisecond boots and a minimal attack surface, and can accept its limits.

blocks.question: A team needs fork, strace and a shell for its service, but wants VMs that boot in tens of milliseconds and strong tenant isolation. Which option fits best?
options: A Unikraft image in binary-compatibility mode
A MirageOS rewrite
A specialized minimal Linux kernel (Lupine-style Kconfig) on a lightweight VMM such as Firecracker
gVisor, because it is the fastest to boot of all VMs
blocks.explain: fork and strace need real Linux. A Kconfig-specialized Linux on a lightweight VMM booted in 23 ms in Lupine's evaluation and keeps hardware isolation. Unikraft offers vfork plus execve but no copying fork; MirageOS is OCaml only; gVisor is a user-space kernel, not a VM.

blocks.question: On UKL, Redis linked unmodified into the kernel gained only modestly, but after it was changed to call internal kernel routines directly (a custom path inside the kernel) it gained 26% throughput. Given Lupine's finding, where did most of that 26% come from?
options: From removing the user/kernel mode switch, which the unmodified build still paid
From running on bare metal instead of in a VM
From skipping the general system call path and its generic layers, a specialization of the work done per request
From UKL's multi-core support
blocks.explain: The unmodified UKL build already runs at supervisor privilege, so the crossing is gone and the gain is modest, as Lupine found with KML. The large gain needed the shortcut, which does less work per request. Specialization, not the crossing, carries the gain. UKL's 26% was measured against Linux in the same setting.

blocks.question: Which property does UKL keep that a MirageOS unikernel gives up?
options: A single address space for the application and kernel
Multi-core execution and other processes running beside the linked application
Running the application at supervisor privilege
Static linking of the application with the kernel
blocks.explain: UKL links one application into Linux at supervisor privilege, like a unikernel, but keeps Linux's SMP support and lets ordinary processes run beside it. Mirage runs one vCPU and one program per VM.
